response.answer: The following only summarizes this historical book: Podophyllum peltatum L. (Taiwan public name: 盾葉鬼臼) [E1]. Podophyllin can be used for habitual constipation [E1]. It can be given as a single drastic purgative or repeatedly for habitual constipation, particularly in cases of liver dysfunction, chronic vomiting after meals, and hypochondria with insomnia [E1]. Due to the colic easily caused by Podophyllin, combination with Extractum Hyoscyami or Extractum Belladonnae is advisable [E1]. This is not modern medical or safety advice.

The following only summarizes this historical book: Piscidia piscipula (non-Taiwan Traditional-Chinese fallback: 毒魚豆) [E1]. The book mentions *Piscidia piscipula* (毒魚豆) [E1]. This plant is a tree that grows 6-8 meters high with smooth, light bark and irregularly spreading branches [E2]. Its leaves are alternate, odd-pinnately compound, with two to four pairs of lateral leaflets [E2]. The entire leaf can be up to 15 cm long, with about 7 cm of this length being the petiole, and another 7 cm being the leaf surface from the first pair of leaflets [E2]. The base of the petiole, about 1-2 cm long, is swollen, and the petiole itself is round, only slightly grooved on the upper side [E2]. The individual leaflets are also sessile [E2].

*Piscidia piscipula* grows in plains and hilly regions of the West Indies, northern South America, and southern North America [E3]. It is found in the Antilles, especially Jamaica, in Mexico, Texas, and Florida [E3]. It thrives in thickets, preferably on volcanic soil near the sea [E3].

Among the indigenous people of Jamaica, Manaka, and St. Vincent, where the tree is called Murungi or Mulungs, it has long been known as a poison [E4]. The Dominican monk Jean Baptiste Labat recounted in 1722 that the sap of the plant was used to poison hunting arrows on the Antilles [E4]. Animals struck by these arrows would immediately become stunned and die without their flesh becoming inedible [E4].

A. G. Nagle isolated a bitter substance from the plant's constituents, which he named Piscidin, with the formula C16H15O8 [E5]. To prepare it, the fluid extract is mixed with some lime paste and digested in a warm place for half an hour [E5]. The mixture is then pressed, filtered, and the filtrate is diluted with water until it begins to cloud, after which the whole is set aside for several days [E5]. Piscidin then separates out in small, colorless prisms, which can be purified by recrystallization from alcohol [E5]. The substance melts at 192° and is insoluble in water [E5]. This is not modern medical or safety advice.
